title: Douglas v. Deutsche Bank National Trust Co., No. 24-CV-1099, Published Order

reading.body:
This is a case of a model asserting something false as fact, and of that assertion reaching a court. The Reuters headline records a DC court faulting lawyers for a Deutsche Bank subsidiary over an AI hallucination, and the second document is the published order in Douglas v. Deutsche Bank National Trust Co., No. 24-CV-1099. The failure sits with the lawyers' use of AI output in a matter before the court, a setting where every factual claim is expected to be traceable to a source. Catching it would have taken a person checking the assertion against the underlying record instead of treating fluent output as verified.

The catalogue entry shows a second failure of its own. Its summary field holds a system message rather than a summary of the reporting, so the record does not carry the underlying facts. That is a document handling failure at the point where the order was passed to a summarisation step, and it means the substance of the order is not established by anything given here.

What is not established: the contents of the order, whether the hallucination appeared in a filing or in some other submission, whether any penalty followed, and whether anyone intended to mislead. A court faulting lawyers is a judicial action reported by an outlet, and a report is not proof of intent.
